sections.title: In brief
sections.text: Knight shifts attention from generating designs within a style to generating new design languages by changing the spatial relations that support them.

sections.title: Question
sections.text: Can existing compositional knowledge become a systematic starting point for invention?

sections.title: Premise and claim
sections.text: Replacing constituent shapes inside known spatial relations yields new relations from which new grammars can be constructed.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Define a two-way shape-equivalence rule with a specified geometric alignment. Apply it repeatedly to shapes in a spatial relation; parameterized schemata handle families of shapes.

sections.title: Examples
sections.text: Square–triangle and rectangle–trapezoid examples produce alternative relation families. Round-to-pointed arch replacement gives a deliberately elementary Romanesque–Gothic comparison.

sections.title: What follows
sections.text: Repeated replacements can define finite or infinite classes of spatial relations. These supply multiple possible languages, rather than merely variants of one finished drawing.

sections.title: Limits
sections.text: A design or corpus permits several grammatical interpretations. The paper proposes descriptive possibilities; it does not establish that historical designers consciously used these replacement rules.

sections.title: Why read it
sections.text: Distinguish changing a design with a rule from changing the relations used to design an entire grammar.

reading_path.label: Understand what a language means here

terms.meaning: A reversible replacement specifying both shapes and their alignment in a spatial relation.
